sonuc: Violation of Article 8 - Right to respect for private and family life (Article 8-1 - Respect for correspondence)
paragraflar: CASE OF PEKSAK v. TÜRKİYE
(Application no. 52433/21)
This judgment is final but it may be subject to editorial revision.
In the case of Peksak v. Türkiye,
The European Court of Human Rights (Second Section), sitting as a Committee composed of:
Oddný Mjöll Arnardóttir, President, Gediminas Sagatys, Juha Lavapuro, judges, and Dorothee von Arnim, Deputy Section Registrar,

the application (no. 52433/21) against the Republic of Türkiye lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) on 13 October 2021 by a Turkish national, Mr Ali Efendi Peksak (“the applicant”), who was born in 1969 and is detained in Bolu, and was represented by Mr T. Önay, a lawyer practising in Istanbul;

The decision to give notice of the complaint concerning Article 8 of the Convention to the Turkish Government (“the Government”), represented by their then Agent, Mr Hacı Ali Açıkgül, former Head of the Department of Human Rights of the Ministry of Justice of the Republic of Türkiye, and to declare the remainder of the application inadmissible;
the parties’ observations;
the decision to reject the Government’s objection to the examination of the case by a Committee;
Having deliberated in private on 20 October 2026,
Delivers the following judgment, which was adopted on that date:
SUBJECT MATTER OF THE CASE
1. The application concerns the monitoring of the applicant’s correspondence with his lawyer by the prison authorities.

2. At the material time the applicant was detained pending trial in the Kocaeli Second T-Type Closed Penal Institution (“the penitentiary institution”) on charges of membership of the organisation described by the Turkish authorities as the “Fetullahist Terror Organisation/Parallel State Structure” (FETÖ/PDY).

3. On 25 December 2018 the applicant applied to the Kocaeli enforcement judge, complaining that a letter sent to him by his lawyer, which had arrived at the penitentiary institution on 20 December 2018 (“the first letter”), had been delivered only after it had been opened and inspected by the prison authorities.

4. On 7 February 2019 the Kocaeli enforcement judge dismissed the complaint on the grounds that it had not been possible for the prison administration to determine whether such letter had actually been sent by the applicant’s lawyer.

5. On 15 February 2019 the applicant lodged an objection against that decision with the Kocaeli First Assize Court, which rejected his objection on 25 February 2019 on the grounds that there had been no procedural or legal irregularity in the decision of the Kocaeli enforcement judge.

6. On 9 April 2019 the applicant lodged an individual application with the Constitutional Court, complaining, inter alia, that his right to respect for correspondence had been violated on account of the monitoring of correspondence with his lawyer. On 10 September 2021 the Constitutional Court dismissed the application as being manifestly ill-founded, holding that, in view of the documents submitted, there had been no interference with the rights and freedoms provided in the Constitution or that the interference in question had not amounted to a violation.

7. On 29 January 2019 the applicant lodged another complaint with the Kocaeli enforcement judge, alleging that another letter sent to him on 23 January 2019 by his lawyer had also been opened and inspected by the prison authorities. Subsequently, on 10 April 2019 the Kocaeli enforcement judge decided that there was no need to deliver a decision on that application, as a decision had already been delivered by the court on a similar complaint which had previously been lodged. The applicant neither appealed against that decision nor lodged an application with the Constitutional Court in respect of the second alleged interference.
8. Relying on Articles 8 and 9 of the Convention, the applicant complained about the monitoring of his correspondence with his lawyer.
ALLEGED VIOLATION OF ARTICLE 8 OF THE CONVENTION

9. Having regard to the formulation of the applicant’s complaint and the nature of the measure in issue, the Court considers that it is appropriate to examine the facts complained of solely from the standpoint of Article 8 of the Convention (compare Radomilja and Others v. Croatia [GC], nos. 37685/10 and 22768/12, § 126, 20 March 2018).

10. The Government raised various preliminary objections. First, they submitted that the applicant had never initiated a new action against the decision of the Kocaeli enforcement judge delivered on 10 April 2019 (see paragraph 7 above) and that the applicant had failed to raise a complaint concerning that decision before the Constitutional Court. Therefore, they submitted that the application should be declared inadmissible for non‑exhaustion of domestic remedies.

11. The Government further invited the Court to declare the application inadmissible on account of lack of significant disadvantage within the meaning of Article 35 § 3 (b) of the Convention. They argued that the applicant had neither suffered any financial disadvantage nor had he mentioned that he had suffered any non-pecuniary disadvantage on account of the impugned measure. They further submitted that the applicant had had the opportunity to gain information from the outside world via different channels. They also noted that the letters had been delivered to the applicant without any damage.

12. The Government further asserted that the application was manifestly ill‑founded, arguing that the national judicial authorities had duly examined the applicant’s complaints in compliance with procedural rules and there was no reason to call into question their findings.

13. Concerning the first objection, the Court observes that the applicant raised before the Constitutional Court his claim regarding the first letter, to the effect that there had been, in substance, a violation of the Convention on account of the monitoring of his correspondence with his lawyer (see paragraph 6 above). The Court further notes that the applicant had exhausted all the domestic remedies before lodging his application with the Court regarding the first letter. It therefore dismisses the Government’s objection of non-exhaustion of domestic remedies in this regard.

14. Regarding the second letter, the Court notes that the applicant failed to exhaust domestic remedies by not appealing against the decision delivered by the Kocaeli enforcement judge on 10 April 2019 and subsequently by not lodging an individual application in respect of the proceedings regarding this letter (see paragraph 7 above). Therefore, the Court considers that the Government’s objection must be upheld with regard to the second letter and that the application must be declared inadmissible for non-exhaustion of domestic remedies in that regard.

15. As to the Government’s objection concerning lack of a significant disadvantage, the Court stresses the privileged nature of the lawyer-client relationship and the importance of respect for lawyer-client confidentiality in the light of its well-established case-law (see Campbell v. the United Kingdom, 25 March 1992, §§ 32-54, Series A no. 233; Ekinci and Akalın v. Turkey, no. 77097/01, § 47, 30 January 2007; and Eylem Kaya v. Turkey, no. 26623/07, §§ 41 et seq., 13 December 2016). Therefore, the Court considers that the applicant can be considered to have suffered a significant disadvantage on account of the monitoring of the letter sent by his lawyer. Accordingly, this objection under Article 35 § 3 (b) of the Convention must be rejected (see, mutatis mutandis, Canavcı and Others v. Türkiye, nos. 24074/19 and 2 others, § 79, 14 November 2023).

16. The Court further considers that the arguments put forward by the Government concerning their objection in respect of the allegedly manifestly ill‑founded nature of the application raise issues requiring an examination of the merits of the complaint under Article 8 of the Convention (compare also Uygun v. Türkiye, no. 9389/19, § 49, 3 June 2025).

17. The Court notes that the applicant’s complaint with regard to the first letter is neither manifestly ill-founded nor inadmissible on any other of the grounds listed in Article 35 of the Convention. This part of the application must therefore be declared admissible.

18. Relying on the principle of lawyer-client confidentiality, the applicant argued that under Turkish law, communications between a lawyer and his or her client in detention could not be subjected to any restriction. The applicant further emphasised that the envelope of the first letter had borne a stamp indicating that it had come from a lawyer’s office and had included the lawyer’s office telephone number and address, and that the envelope containing the letter had been sealed with a distinctively coloured special label.

19. As regards the existence of an interference with the right to respect for correspondence with a lawyer, the Government argued that there had been no indication on the envelope of the first letter that its sender, T.O., was the applicant’s lawyer.

20. The Government asserted that the impugned letter had been sent by post from outside the penitentiary institutions and enclosed in an envelope, and that it had been subjected to a basic examination on security grounds to determine who had sent it and whether it had posed a danger to the security of the penitentiary institution, in accordance with the relevant legislation. They submitted that the practice was prescribed by section 68 of Law no. 5275 and Article 91 of the by-law in force at the material time.
21. The Government further argued that the interference had pursued the aims of ensuring the security of penitentiary institutions and protecting the rights of convicted persons and detainees.

22. The Government lastly submitted that it was necessary in a democratic society not to deliver to the prisoners uncontrolled correspondence which might allow them to communicate with illegal organisations.

23. The general principles concerning the right to respect for a person’s correspondence with his or her lawyer have been set out in Campbell (cited above, §§ 32-54), Ekinci and Akalın (cited above, § 47) and Eylem Kaya (cited above, § 41).

24. The Court observes that the Government have submitted no document or argument to refute the applicant’s submission that the letter sent by his lawyer was opened and that the envelope in question bore the name of its sender, T.O. and indicated that he was a lawyer. It notes that it is uncontested that T.O. was the applicant’s lawyer. Therefore, it considers that the letter sent to the applicant by his lawyer was opened in the present case. It concludes that such practice by the prison authorities constituted an interference with the applicant’s right to respect for his correspondence with his lawyer within the meaning of Article 8 § 1 of the Convention (see Campbell, cited above, § 33; Ekinci and Akalın, cited above, §§ 37-38; and Eylem Kaya, cited above, §§ 27-28).

25. As to whether the interference was prescribed by law, the Court takes note of the Government’s submission that the interference was prescribed by section 68 of Law No. 5275 and section 91 of the by-law in force at the material time (see, for the text of these provisions, Eylem Kaya, cited above, §§ 16-17). While doubts may arise as to the compatibility of the impugned measure with the relevant provisions in the present case, the Court will proceed on the assumption that the interference was prescribed by law (ibid., §§ 32-35), having regard to the conclusion it reaches regarding the necessity of the interference (see paragraph 27 below). It also accepts that the interference pursued legitimate aims under Article 8 § 2 of the Convention, in particular the safeguarding of “national security” and/or “the prevention of disorder or crime” (see, mutatis mutandis, Erdem v. Germany, no. 38321/97, § 60, ECHR 2001-VII (excerpts), and Eylem Kaya, cited above, § 39).

26. As regards the necessity of the measure in dispute, the Court reiterates that under Article 8 of the Convention a privileged regime must be applied to correspondence between a lawyer and a detainee, whatever its purpose (see Eylem Kaya, cited above, § 41, and the case-law cited therein). The confidentiality of correspondence between detainees and their lawyers constitutes a fundamental right of individuals and directly affects their right to mount a defence. A limitation of this right is therefore permissible only in exceptional circumstances and must be surrounded by adequate and effective safeguards against abuse (ibid., § 44), such as entrusting any necessary control of correspondence to independent judges and not to the prison authorities themselves (ibid., § 45).

27. The Court considers that it has not been demonstrated in the present case that the monitoring and interception by the prison authorities of the correspondence between the applicant and his lawyer was carried out in such exceptional circumstances. In particular, the Government have not alleged any concrete indications of abuse in the context of this correspondence. It has further not been demonstrated that the monitoring and interception of the correspondence was surrounded by the necessary safeguards against abuse. Accordingly, this interference was not “necessary in a democratic society” within the meaning of Article 8 § 2 (see Eylem Kaya, cited above, §§ 47-48).
28. There has accordingly been a violation of Article 8 of the Convention.
APPLICATION OF ARTICLE 41 OF THE CONVENTION

29. The applicant claimed 50,000 euros (EUR) in respect of non‑pecuniary damage and EUR 1,000 in respect of costs and expenses. He submitted a contract prepared by his representative and signed by the parties in which the representation fee was set at EUR 1,000.
30. The Government disputed those claims.

31. In respect of non-pecuniary damage, the Court considers that, in the circumstances of the present case, the finding of a violation constitutes in itself just satisfaction for any non-pecuniary damage sustained by the applicant.

32. Having regard to the documents in its possession, the Court considers it reasonable to award EUR 250 covering costs and expenses under all heads, plus any tax that may be chargeable to the applicant.
FOR THESE REASONS, THE COURT, UNANIMOUSLY,
Declares the application admissible regarding the first letter sent to the applicant, and inadmissible regarding the second letter sent to him;
Holds that there has been a violation of Article 8 of the Convention regarding the first letter sent to the applicant;
Holds that the finding of a violation constitutes in itself sufficient just satisfaction for any non-pecuniary damage sustained by the applicant;

that the respondent State is to pay the applicant, within three months, EUR 250 (two hundred and fifty euros), plus any tax that may be chargeable to the applicant, in respect of costs and expenses, to be converted into the currency of the respondent State at the rate applicable at the date of settlement;

that from the expiry of the above-mentioned three months until settlement simple interest shall be payable on the above amount at a rate equal to the marginal lending rate of the European Central Bank during the default period plus three percentage points;
Dismisses the remainder of the applicant’s claim for just satisfaction.
Done in English, and notified in writing on 17 November 2026, pursuant to Rule 77 §§ 2 and 3 of the Rules of Court.
Dorothee von Arnim Oddný Mjöll Arnardóttir Deputy Registrar President
